title: Motor types
creator: Texas Instruments
watch_for: Compare how brushed DC, stepper, and brushless DC motors produce rotation. For each, identify what switches the winding current and what additional electronics the mechanism needs.
takeaway: The motor technology changes the driver and feedback work you must supply. A servo is a controlled system that can use different motor technologies, so keep that choice separate from the motor family.
limits: A motor-family introduction, not a continuous-torque comparison or a selection of parts for our joint. Use the later torque-speed, thermal, and feedback checks to narrow the choice.

title: Microstepping in bipolar stepper motors
creator: Texas Instruments
watch_for: Compare the phase-current waveforms for full stepping, half-stepping, and microstepping. Notice that smaller commanded increments come from intermediate current combinations.
takeaway: Microstepping can improve motion smoothness, but command resolution alone does not establish loaded accuracy. Available torque, friction, current regulation, and the speed-torque curve still constrain the design.
limits: The waveform lesson is not a guarantee that every microstep produces equal mechanical motion, and it does not establish an assembled stage's accuracy or thermal limits.

title: Modern Robotics, Chapter 8.9: Actuation, Gearing, and Friction
creator: Northwestern Robotics — Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park
watch_for: Follow the motor rotor and the slower output separately. Watch how substituting motor speed into kinetic energy makes rotor inertia at the output scale with the square of the reduction ratio.
takeaway: Reduction helps a small motor create output torque, but greater reduction can make the output harder to accelerate from an external push. Torque multiplication and mechanical responsiveness must be compared together.
limits: The dynamics explanation does not select a gearbox or establish its friction, backdrivability, bearing capacity, or life. The source page includes a written transcript.

title: Harmonic Drive® strain wave gear - zero backlash
creator: Harmonic Drive LLC
watch_for: Identify the wave generator, flexible toothed cup, and rigid outer spline. Follow the moving engagement regions while the flexible output advances much more slowly than the input.
takeaway: A small tooth-count difference can create a large reduction in a compact package. The price is a demanding flexible component and precision engagement geometry; a printed demonstration does not inherit a commercial reducer's performance.
limits: The title and product claims describe this manufacturer's technology. Zero backlash does not mean zero elastic deflection, and catalog ratings must not be transferred to a new material or geometry.

title: Tech Tips: Ball vs. Lead Screw Technology
creator: Thomson Industries
watch_for: Compare the sliding contact of a lead screw with the rolling contact of a ball screw. Relate that contact mechanism to efficiency, duty, maintenance, and the choice of a complete linear actuator.
takeaway: A ball screw can reduce drive loss; a lead screw can simplify and reduce the cost of a modest-duty axis. Choose from actual load, speed, life, and support requirements instead of assuming one family is always better.
limits: Manufacturer examples are product-specific. Neither a low lead nor this comparison proves power-off holding, and the screw still needs a separate guide and a suitable axial support arrangement. Opens on Thomson's video page.

title: SDM Hand
creator: Yale Grablab
watch_for: Watch how the fingers conform as different links make contact with an object. Separate the number of moving finger joints from the number of independently controlled motions.
takeaway: Tendons and underactuation can let simple drive arrangements adapt to object shape. They trade independent joint control for behavior that depends on routing, compliance, friction, and contact geometry.
limits: This is the SDM-hand demonstration linked by Yale OpenHand, not the guide's single-finger design. It does not establish equal fingertip forces, a payload rating for our model, or independent control of every joint.

title: Basic pneumatics for process automation
creator: Festo SA
watch_for: Identify the air supply, pneumatic actuator, and pilot or directional valve as separate parts. Distinguish the electrical command to a valve from the pressure that produces actuator force.
takeaway: Pneumatics can suit repeated industrial actuation when an air supply is available. The comparison with electric actuation must include that supply, valves, flow limits, compressibility, leaks, and the required positioning behavior.
limits: A process-automation training session, not a portable-robot component selection or an instruction to build an unqualified pressure system. Playback remains hosted by the creator on YouTube.

title: Brushless-DC basics
creator: Texas Instruments
watch_for: Connect the motor's magnetic construction to the circuit that switches winding current. Identify the commutation problem the electronics must solve before an outer loop can control the robot's position.
takeaway: Moving commutation into electronics removes brushes but adds a drive-and-sensing design problem. Slow reversal, controlled torque at rest, and a robot's feedback requirements need explicit support from the selected controller.
limits: BLDC fundamentals do not establish that an arbitrary fan ESC can perform robot-joint position or torque control. Verify the actual drive's sensing, startup, current, and regenerative-energy behavior.
